intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note under a slide explains why it matters, how to remember it and where people slip. Work the exercises in pencil, check yourself with the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins beside mine.

sections.title: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability
sections.big_idea: A disaster is a hazard meeting people who cannot cope, so **risk is hazard × exposure × vulnerability** and each term needs its own action.
in_plain_words: The law defines a disaster by the community's coping capacity. The same cyclone is weather over an empty sea and a disaster over a village with no shelter and no warning. The wind is identical. What differs is who stands in its path and what they have to protect themselves.

Practice therefore separates three things that news reports run together. The hazard is the physical event, exposure is who and what sits in the place, and vulnerability is the set of conditions that decide how badly they are hurt. **A programme that does not say which term it changes** usually cannot show that it worked.

diagram.note: if any one term falls towards zero, risk falls towards zero

key_terms.meaning: The physical process or event that may cause harm.
People and assets located in hazard-prone areas.
Conditions that raise susceptibility to harm from a hazard.
Potential loss over a period, a function of the other terms.
Ability to resist, absorb, respond to and recover from a hazard.
What a community can handle with its own means.

worked_example.title: Score two blocks on one hazard
worked_example.setup: Illustrative scores on a 1 to 5 scale. Both blocks face a cyclone hazard of 4. Block A scores exposure 2 and vulnerability 1. Block B scores exposure 3 and vulnerability 3.
steps: Block A: 4 × 2 = 8, then 8 × 1 = 8.
Now give B a nearby shelter and a warning in the local language, which cuts its vulnerability from 3 to 1.
Block B again: 12 × 1 = 12.
The hazard never changed. Only the vulnerability term moved.
worked_example.answer: B falls from 36 to 12 by changing vulnerability alone, with the hazard untouched.

mistakes: Calling the hazard the disaster. A disaster needs people unable to cope.
Reporting one district death toll, which averages a well-protected village with a badly exposed one.
Naming a programme 'disaster risk reduction' without saying which of the three terms it changes.
Forgetting slow hazards such as drought and heat, which harm through lost income over months.

recall.q: Which clause of the DM Act definition carries the idea that runs through the course?
recall.a: The clause saying the harm is beyond the coping capacity of the community.

recall.q: Give one action that lowers exposure and one that lowers vulnerability.
recall.a: Moving a village out of a floodplain lowers exposure; a shelter with timely warning lowers vulnerability.

recall.q: What did the Sixteenth Finance Commission use to measure exposure and vulnerability?
recall.a: Projected State population for exposure and State per-capita income for vulnerability.

recall.q: Which hazard group is financed worst, and what evidence does the deck give?
recall.a: Slow-onset hazards: heat was not on the national notified list, and drought took 17.26 per cent of State spending against 55.09 for floods.

recall.q: What is the last of the five questions to ask of any programme?
recall.a: What happens to the person who cannot read the warning, cannot walk to the shelter or will lose a day's wage by going.

sections.title: The Sendai Framework 2015-2030
sections.big_idea: Sendai is a **voluntary global yardstick**: one goal, seven targets and four priorities, reported by countries against 38 indicators.
in_plain_words: Adopted on 18 March 2015, Sendai replaced the Hyogo Framework. Its main shift was from managing disasters to managing risk, so action comes before the event as well as after it. It binds no one, so its force comes from countries reporting their own numbers.

The goal reads as three instructions: prevent new risk, reduce existing risk and strengthen resilience. The first is the cheapest and the most often ignored. The seven targets split into outcomes, which are measured with loss data, and **means**, which are strategies, cooperation and early warning.

spokes.label: Seven targets
spokes.sub: a to d outcomes, e to g means

key_terms.meaning: The 2015-2030 voluntary UN agreement on disaster risk reduction.
The 2005-2015 predecessor that Sendai replaced.
The UN office that supports implementation, follow-up and review.
Using recovery to reduce future risk, from priority 4.
The online system countries report against.
A tool for building disaster loss databases.

worked_example.title: Sort the seven targets
worked_example.setup: A colleague asks which targets are outcomes and which are means. Work through the list in order.
steps: Target (a) mortality: an outcome, counted with loss data.
Target (b) affected people: an outcome.
Target (c) economic loss: an outcome. Target (d) damage to infrastructure and services: an outcome.
Targets (e) strategies, (f) cooperation and (g) early warning: means.
Check the count: 4 + 3 = 7.
worked_example.answer: Targets a to d are outcomes and e to g are means, four and three, seven in all.

mistakes: Treating Sendai as binding. It creates no obligations.
Reading a country's low heat-death count as success, when the records may be incomplete.
Funding only response, which keeps paying for risk that planning created.
Leaving caste off the list of groups, because the framework does not name it.

recall.q: When was Sendai adopted and what did it replace?
recall.a: On 18 March 2015, replacing the Hyogo Framework for Action 2005-2015.

recall.q: Which target has an earlier deadline and why?
recall.a: Target (e), national and local strategies, by 2020, because strategies had to exist before outcomes could move.

recall.q: What are the four priorities?
recall.a: Understanding risk, strengthening governance, investing in resilience, and preparedness with Build Back Better.

recall.q: Why is self-reporting a weakness?
recall.a: Loss databases are only as complete as the records that feed them, so a country with few recorded deaths may look better than it is.

recall.q: Which groups does the framework name?
recall.a: Women, children and youth, persons with disabilities, poor people, migrants, indigenous peoples, volunteers and older persons.

sections.title: India's disaster law and institutions
sections.big_idea: The DM Act 2005 puts a body and a plan at **every level**, and the 2025 amendment added definitions, audits and urban authorities.
in_plain_words: Before 2005 India handled disasters through relief codes run by State relief commissioners. The Act gave the subject a statute, permanent bodies at each level, written plans, a specialist force and funds. The chairs show where authority sits: the Prime Minister nationally, the Chief Minister in the State and the Collector in the district.

The district body does most of the work, and the 2025 amendment added to the tiers: an Urban Authority chaired by the Municipal Commissioner, a State Disaster Response Force and statutory national committees. **Read the Act with its critics**: the government points to clearer definitions and data, while a critic sees more central control.

children.label: National
items: NDMA, chaired by the Prime Minister

children.label: State
items: SDMA, chaired by the Chief Minister

diagram.caption: a body at every level, each with a chair

key_terms.meaning: National Disaster Management Authority, chaired by the Prime Minister.
State Disaster Management Authority, chaired by the Chief Minister.
District authority chaired by the Collector, with an elected co-chair.
National Crisis Management Committee, made statutory in 2025.
Cabinet body that approves central assistance, s. 8B.
National and State records the 2025 amendment requires.

worked_example.title: Trace the money after a severe cyclone
worked_example.setup: A State is hit by a cyclone of severe nature. Put the steps in order.
steps: The State meets the first costs from its State Disaster Response Fund. It can spend this at once.
The State submits a memorandum seeking central assistance.
An Inter-Ministerial Central Team visits and assesses the damage.
The Inter-Ministerial Group under the Union Home Secretary scrutinises the assessment.
The High Level Committee approves assistance from the National Disaster Response Fund.
worked_example.answer: State fund, memorandum, central team, Inter-Ministerial Group, High Level Committee. Central money waits for four steps.

mistakes: Confusing the two NDRFs: the National Disaster Response Force (s. 44) and the National Disaster Response Fund (s. 46). SDRF has the same double meaning.
Assuming every State has an Urban Disaster Management Authority. The Act says a State may create one.
Citing s. 61 as if it still covers compensation. The 2025 text names relief only.
Using a district plan that has not been updated and lists only departments and phone numbers.

recall.q: Who chairs the NDMA, the SDMA and the DDMA?
recall.a: The Prime Minister, the Chief Minister and the Collector or District Magistrate, with an elected co-chair at district level.

recall.q: Which provision bans discrimination in relief, and on what grounds?
recall.a: Section 61: sex, caste, community, descent or religion.

recall.q: How often must district plans now be reviewed?
recall.a: At least every two years.

recall.q: What does s. 60A allow?
recall.a: The Union or a State may by notification require anyone to act or refrain in relation to a hazard for up to six months, with a penalty up to ₹10,000.

recall.q: What is the main criticism in the EPW commentary?
recall.a: That the amendment centralises authority and gives local governments no larger role or money.

sections.title: Paying for disasters: the funds
sections.big_idea: Four statutory funds pay for disasters, and **response money moves fast while mitigation money moves slowly**.
in_plain_words: There are two funds nationally and two in each State, one for response and one for mitigation. The Finance Commission decides how much goes in each five-year period. States contribute 25 per cent of their funds and the Union 75, or 10 and 90 for north-eastern and Himalayan States.

The Sixteenth Commission shares money among States 70 per cent by past spending and 30 per cent by a risk index. Relief spending shows who is reached: over half went to agricultural inputs. **Landless workers and sick people** appear in no line. Mitigation funds were created under the Fifteenth Commission but release ran near 80 per cent against 95 to 100 for response.

left.title: Response funds
items: First call after a notified disaster

key_terms.meaning: State Disaster Response Fund, first call after a notified disaster.
National fund for central assistance after severe disasters.
Money for projects that reduce future risk, national or State.
Body that sets fund allocations for each five-year award.
Disasters the Union lists as payable from the national funds.
FC-16 score multiplying hazard, exposure and vulnerability.

worked_example.title: Split an illustrative State allocation
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a State is allocated ₹800 crore for 2026-31 across its response and mitigation funds. Apply the shares the deck gives.
steps: Union share at 75 per cent: 800 × 75 ÷ 100 = 600.
State share at 25 per cent: 800 × 25 ÷ 100 = 200.
Response fund at 80 per cent: 800 × 80 ÷ 100 = 640.
Mitigation fund at 20 per cent: 800 × 20 ÷ 100 = 160.
If the State were north-eastern, the Union share at 90 per cent would be 800 × 90 ÷ 100 = 720.
worked_example.answer: ₹600 crore Union and ₹200 crore State; ₹640 crore response and ₹160 crore mitigation; ₹720 crore Union for a 90:10 State.

mistakes: Quoting rising allocations as progress. The figures are nominal and show allocation only, with no release or spending.
Assuming heat and lightning are on the national list. They were only recommended.
Moving money between response and mitigation funds. They are separate funds under the Act.
Reading State per-capita income as district vulnerability. Poor districts in richer States stay invisible.

recall.q: What are the four statutory funds?
recall.a: The National Disaster Response Fund, the National Disaster Mitigation Fund, and the State response and State mitigation funds.

recall.q: How does FC-16 share money among States?
recall.a: 70 per cent on average past disaster spending and 30 per cent on the Disaster Risk Index.

recall.q: What share of relief spending went to agricultural inputs and ex gratia?
recall.a: 55.6 per cent and 23.4 per cent.

recall.q: How much of SDRF can a State spend on locally notified disasters?
recall.a: Up to 10 per cent.

recall.q: What is the opening for a district practitioner?
recall.a: Mitigation money is under-used, so a proposal with a hazard, a costed project and a monitoring plan fits what the funds were waiting for.

sections.title: Cyclones and Odisha's record
sections.big_idea: Odisha cut cyclone deaths from nearly 10,000 to the low tens by building a **whole system**, yet its own report shows who it still missed.
in_plain_words: Odisha faces more cyclone landfalls than almost anywhere in the subcontinent and is poor and rural, so its record is a test of what preparedness can do. After the 1999 super cyclone it built a State authority, a rescue force, multipurpose shelters with community task forces, and a siren and SMS warning chain to the last mile.

The results are deaths of 44, none, 61 and 64 in four later storms, and 15.5 lakh people moved in about a day for Fani. **Losses are still large**, and the State's own assessment found that relief tied to ration cards left out migrants and that shelters were segregated. A system that saves lives can still share relief unequally.

diagram.caption: a system built over two decades

key_terms.meaning: Odisha State Disaster Management Authority, set up after 1999.
Odisha Disaster Rapid Action Force, a trained State rescue force.
A strong public building used in cyclones and floods.
Runs the State Emergency Operation Centre all year.
The three figures a post-disaster assessment reports.
Maternity waiting homes used before Fani for pregnant women.

worked_example.title: Read the Fani figures
worked_example.setup: Use the numbers in the deck: deaths in 1999 nearly 10,000 and in Fani 64; Fani damage ₹16,465 crore and loss ₹7,712 crore; 3.62 lakh houses damaged, 95 per cent of them in Puri, Khordha and Cuttack.
steps: How many times smaller are Fani deaths? 10,000 ÷ 64 = 156.25, so about 156 times.
Damage and loss together: 16,465 + 7,712 = 24,177 crore.
Houses in the three districts: 362,000 × 95 ÷ 100 = 343,900.
Deaths fell a hundredfold while the bill stayed large, which is the section's two-sided message.
worked_example.answer: About 156 times fewer deaths, ₹24,177 crore of damage and loss, and about 343,900 houses in three districts.

mistakes: Crediting one component, such as sirens, for the fall in deaths. The record cannot split the effect.
Treating zero deaths as zero loss. Losses from cyclones are rising.
Tying cash and grain to ration cards, which leaves out migrants and kiln workers.
Placing shelters by convenience instead of near the poorest hamlets.

recall.q: Which year's cyclone started Odisha's institution building?
recall.a: The super cyclone of October 1999.

recall.q: How many people were evacuated for Fani, and to how many shelters?
recall.a: 15.5 lakh people to 9,177 shelters, including 879 multipurpose shelters.

recall.q: What two exclusions did the Fani assessment record?
recall.a: Relief tied to ration cards that left out migrants and kiln workers, and segregated arrangements in shelters.

recall.q: How many days did Fani meander before landfall?
recall.a: Eleven days.

recall.q: Which rows of the lessons table are about unfinished work?
recall.a: Relief through ration cards and housing reconstruction, which concern livelihoods and dignity.

sections.title: Floods, landslides and lightning
sections.big_idea: Floods take the money, but **lightning takes the lives**, and each hazard needs a warning matched to its clock.
in_plain_words: Floods took 55.09 per cent of State disaster spending. They come in different forms with different lead times: days for rivers and surge, minutes to hours for flash floods and glacial lakes, hours for urban floods. Embankments protect some people and endanger others, especially those living between the wall and the river.

Landslides take little money because hill States are small, and rainfall thresholds are the practical warning. Lightning was the leading natural cause of death in 2022. It is a hazard where **vulnerability is about work**. Assessments that count only deaths, houses and crops miss lost wages, which fall hardest on daily workers.

left.title: Floods take the money
items: Days of warning for rivers and surge
Costs fall on crops, houses, roads

right.title: Lightning takes the lives
items: Risk is highest for field labourers

key_terms.meaning: A flood that builds over days and can be forecast upstream.
Glacial lake outburst flood, with minutes to hours of warning.
A built defence such as an embankment, dam or channel.
Zoning, warning, insurance, raised houses and similar.
Accumulated rain level known to trigger slides on a slope.
Post-Disaster Needs Assessment, a joint damage, loss and needs study.

worked_example.title: Check the deck's own figures
worked_example.setup: Use the numbers the deck gives for lightning in 2022 and for the Pakistan floods.
steps: Lightning share of deaths from forces of nature: 2,887 ÷ 8,060 = 35.8%.
Deaths from all other forces of nature: 8,060 − 2,887 = 5,173.
Pakistan damage plus losses, in USD billion: 14.9 + 15.2 = 30.1.
Recovery needs were 16.3 billion, so the first two figures alone do not describe what rebuilding costs.
worked_example.answer: Lightning caused 35.8 per cent of such deaths, 5,173 deaths came from other forces, and Pakistan's damage plus losses were USD 30.1 billion.

mistakes: Counting only deaths in a flood assessment, when poverty impact was the larger harm in Pakistan.
Assuming an embankment protects everyone, including the people between it and the river.
Sending lightning warnings by SMS alone, which misses field labourers without phones.
Reading the small landslide share of spending as a small problem.

recall.q: What share of State disaster spending went to floods, 2019-20 to 2023-24?
recall.a: 55.09 per cent.

recall.q: How many people did the Pakistan 2022 floods affect, and what poverty effect was projected?
recall.a: About 33 million; poverty up by 3.7 to 4.0 percentage points, or 8.4 to 9.1 million more people poor.

recall.q: Which hazard led deaths from forces of nature in India in 2022?
recall.a: Lightning, with 2,887 of 8,060 deaths.

recall.q: Why does a breach need its own plan?
recall.a: Water arrives suddenly in places people believed safe, so warning and evacuation cannot assume the embankment holds.

recall.q: Name one thing a flood assessment usually misses.
recall.a: Days of work lost, tenant losses, rented houses, or deaths from disease after the flood.

sections.title: Drought
sections.big_idea: Drought arrives in **four stages over months**, so a response that waits for crop results comes after people have sold their assets.
in_plain_words: Rain fails first, crops fail weeks later and wells and tanks fail months later. Throughout, people sell animals, migrate and borrow. A declaration based on rainfall alone comes early and can miss a district where rain was near normal but badly timed. One that waits for crop-cutting comes late.

Drought harms mainly through lost work and income, so the response that matters is **employment and food over months**. Input subsidy reaches cultivators, while landless labourers need another instrument. A declaration by block or tehsil also decides who is left out, since a village in an undeclared block gets nothing.

diagram.caption: the kinds of drought arrive in this sequence

key_terms.meaning: Rainfall well below normal for a place and season.
Soil moisture too low for crops at the stage they need it.
Reservoirs, rivers and groundwater fall below normal.
Shortfall of water and food that hurts income and nutrition.
A State notification that opens relief norms and central help.
Sixty notified days a year when no guarantee work is undertaken.

worked_example.title: Two numbers on drought money and work
worked_example.setup: Illustrative household, with the deck's figures for the drought earmark: ₹1,200 crore earmarked for twelve drought-prone States, ₹350 crore released by 31 July 2025, and a guarantee of 125 days.
steps: Share released: 350 ÷ 1,200 = 29.2%.
Still unreleased: 1,200 − 350 = 850 crore.
A household has worked 70 of its 125 guaranteed days.
Days remaining: 125 − 70 = 55.
Share of the guarantee used: 70 ÷ 125 = 56%.
worked_example.answer: 29.2 per cent of the earmark was released, leaving ₹850 crore, and the household has used 56 per cent of its guaranteed days.

mistakes: Declaring on rainfall alone, which misses badly timed rain.
Waiting for crop-cutting results, which arrive after people have sold animals and borrowed.
Tying relief to land records, which leaves out tenants, sharecroppers and women farmers without title.
Treating one relief payment as a substitute for months of lost work.

recall.q: What are the four kinds of drought?
recall.a: Meteorological, agricultural, hydrological and socio-economic.

recall.q: What share of State disaster spending went to drought, 2019-20 to 2023-24?
recall.a: 17.26 per cent, second only to floods.

recall.q: How many days does the new rural employment Act guarantee?
recall.a: Not less than 125 days a year to each rural household whose adults volunteer for unskilled work.

recall.q: Why does the unit of declaration matter?
recall.a: Villages inside a block that is not declared get nothing, however badly their own crops failed.

recall.q: Name three indicators of a drought response that move before crop-cutting.
recall.a: Any three of: days of work demanded, fodder prices, livestock sales, migration, school attendance, debt, tanker queues.

sections.title: Heat
sections.big_idea: Heat deaths are **mostly uncounted**, so a good heat plan sets local thresholds, finds the people at risk and measures excess deaths.
in_plain_words: IMD declares a heat wave at 45°C in the plains, but that rule uses dry air temperature only. It says nothing about humidity or hot nights, and people die at lower temperatures where it is humid. Ahmedabad's 2010 heat wave caused 1,344 excess deaths in a month, yet none were recorded as heat deaths.

Ahmedabad's plan ties a 7-day forecast to alerts, health services and outreach, and a pilot evaluation found fewer deaths afterwards, with wide uncertainty. A review of 37 plans found few with local thresholds, targeting or funds, and **none naming its legal authority**. Heat is also an income shock: lost working hours fall hardest on day-wage workers.

diagram.caption: how the Ahmedabad plan runs each season

key_terms.meaning: Maximum at least 40°C and 45°C or more in the plains.
Minimum temperature 4.5°C to 6.4°C above normal.
Lowest temperature reachable by evaporation; combines heat and humidity.
All deaths above the number expected in a normal period.
A local plan that links warnings to health and outreach actions.
Share of hours lost to heat stress, per the ILO.

worked_example.title: Count heat deaths two ways
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: Ahmedabad had 4,462 deaths in May 2010 against a reference of 3,118; NCRB recorded 3,798 heat deaths in India over five years.
steps: Excess deaths in Ahmedabad: 4,462 − 3,118 = 1,344.
Excess as a share of the reference: 1,344 ÷ 3,118 = 43.1%.
NCRB deaths a year: 3,798 ÷ 5 = 759.6, about 760.
One city's single month against the national yearly count: 1,344 ÷ 760 = 1.77 times.
worked_example.answer: 1,344 excess deaths, 43.1 per cent above reference, was about 1.8 times the national yearly count of about 760.

mistakes: Using dry temperature alone as the trigger, which warns the wrong city on the wrong day.
Counting only certified heatstroke deaths, which gives a large undercount.
Copying a template plan without a local vulnerability assessment.
Reading the Ahmedabad evaluation as proof, when it is a one-city before and after comparison.

recall.q: What are the IMD thresholds for a heat wave in the plains?
recall.a: A maximum of at least 40°C, with an actual temperature of 45°C or more, met at two stations for two days.

recall.q: Why does humidity change the danger?
recall.a: As the wet-bulb temperature nears skin temperature, sweating stops working, so humid heat is dangerous at lower readings.

recall.q: What did the Ahmedabad evaluation estimate?
recall.a: 1,190 deaths avoided a year on average, with a 95% interval of 162 to 2,218.

recall.q: What did the review of 37 plans find?
recall.a: Few set local thresholds, nearly all target vulnerable groups poorly, they are underfunded and none states its legal authority.

recall.q: Why is excess all-cause mortality useful?
recall.a: It captures heat deaths certified as other causes, without needing heat on the certificate.

sections.title: Early warning and anticipatory action
sections.big_idea: A warning works only if **every link in the chain holds**, and acting on a forecast means accepting some false alarms.
in_plain_words: An early warning has five links: forecast, warning, dissemination, understanding and action. A failure in any one breaks the chain. Odisha's Fani response shows the whole chain: IMD tracked the storm, the State told Collectors what to do, messages went out in Odia by several channels, and shelters and food were ready.

Warnings travel along ordinary inequality, so each group needs a channel that reaches it. Anticipatory action goes further and releases pre-agreed money when a forecast crosses a threshold. The price is some spending on hazards that turn out weaker. **A system with no false alarms is probably acting too late**, so write down the cost of acting in vain before the season.

nodes.label: Understanding
nodes.sub: trusted, and people know what to do

nodes.label: Action
nodes.sub: in time, with the means to act

diagram.caption: five links, and the weakest one decides

key_terms.meaning: The chain from forecast to protective action by people.
The final stretch where a warning reaches the person.
Pre-agreed, pre-funded steps released when a forecast crosses a threshold.
A forecast, a threshold and an action agreed in advance.
A warning for an event that does not happen.
An event that arrives without a warning.

worked_example.title: An average that hides a hamlet
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a block has ten hamlets of 40 households each. Nine received the cyclone warning in full. One hamlet received nothing.
steps: Households in the block: 10 × 40 = 400.
Households warned: 9 × 40 = 360.
Block coverage: 360 ÷ 400 = 90%.
Coverage in the missed hamlet: 0 ÷ 40 = 0%.
The block report says 90 per cent, and one hamlet has no warning at all.
worked_example.answer: The average is 90 per cent and one hamlet is at 0 per cent, which is why coverage must be reported by group and place.

mistakes: Calling an accurate forecast an early warning system when it reaches only smartphone owners in English.
Setting thresholds so high that no one ever leaves in vain, which means they leave too late.
Assuming a warning works without a list of people who need help to move.
Skipping compensation for the cost of acting, such as lost wages for workers who stop in heat.

recall.q: Name the five links in the warning chain.
recall.a: Forecast, warning, dissemination, understanding and action.

recall.q: What is anticipatory action?
recall.a: Pre-agreed actions with money set aside in advance, released when a forecast crosses a threshold and before the hazard strikes.

recall.q: What happens to trust after repeated false alarms?
recall.a: People stop leaving, so missed events follow from the false alarms.

recall.q: Which channel suits farm labourers in fields?
recall.a: Sirens, loudspeakers, or an employer or supervisor.

recall.q: Which indicator shows how early a warning came?
recall.a: Hours between the first warning received and the hazard's impact.

sections.title: Relief, recovery and who relief misses
sections.big_idea: Relief follows lists, so **whoever is off the list, or low in the hierarchy, is missed**, as the 2004 tsunami and Fani both show.
in_plain_words: Response, rehabilitation, recovery and reconstruction mean different things. Relief is fast and visible, while recovery is slow and underfunded: the recovery window of the national fund had released ₹818.74 crore of ₹20,539 crore by July 2025. A household can be counted as relieved and still be poorer for a decade.

Three records show who is missed. After the 2004 tsunami, Dalits were blocked from aid by others and women were paid through male heads of household. After Fani, cash and rice went only to ration card holders, leaving out migrants and kiln workers. **Count them before the disaster**, because section 61 names caste but not disability or age.

children.label: By gender
items: Ration cards in the male head's name

diagram.caption: every row is a recorded failure in India

key_terms.meaning: Action before, during or after a disaster to save lives.
Restoration of basic services and capacity of a community.
Restoration or improvement of assets, systems and activities.
Rebuilding infrastructure, services and buildings.
A payment made without a legal claim, such as for a death.
Registering adults separately so women are paid directly.

worked_example.title: Measure the gap, and a flat ration
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures: the national response window had released ₹14,855 crore of ₹27,385 crore; the recovery window ₹818.74 crore of ₹20,539 crore. Fani gave 50 kg of rice to every family whatever its size.
steps: Response and Relief window: 14,855 ÷ 27,385 = 54.2%.
Recovery and Reconstruction window: 818.74 ÷ 20,539 = 4.0%.
A family of 3 gets 50 ÷ 3 = 16.67 kg a head.
A family of 6 gets 50 ÷ 6 = 8.33 kg a head.
The flat 50 kg gives the larger family half as much per person.
worked_example.answer: About 54 per cent of the response window was released against 4 per cent for recovery, and a flat ration halves the per-person share for a family of six.

mistakes: Paying relief to the ration card holder, which makes women depend on male relatives.
Using a residence test, which excludes migrants and kiln workers who were equally affected.
Counting only deaths and boats, when labourers lost wages without being counted.
Assuming s. 61 covers disability or age. It names sex, caste, community, descent and religion.

recall.q: What did Human Rights Watch find about caste after the 2004 tsunami?
recall.a: Fishing communities often blocked relief from reaching Dalits, including denying them water.

recall.q: Why were women's claims brokered through men?
recall.a: Ration cards, the main proof of identity and residence, were issued in the name of the male head.

recall.q: Which Fani relief rule excluded migrants?
recall.a: The ₹2,000 and 50 kg of rice went only to ration card holders.

recall.q: What does the new rural employment law allow for relocated people?
recall.a: Registering and getting a job card where they have temporarily relocated, with the work counting towards the 125 days.

recall.q: What is the legal hook for Build Back Better?
recall.a: The Act's definition of recovery, which includes improvement as well as restoration.

sections.title: Insurance and social protection in a shock
sections.big_idea: Match each layer of loss to a **different money source**, and use existing programmes to scale up when a shock hits.
in_plain_words: Losses come in layers by how often they happen. Small frequent losses are paid from savings and social protection, medium ones from State funds, and rare large ones can be passed to insurance or bonds. India mostly relies on public funds, and insurance is nascent except for crop cover.

PMFBY reaches mostly landholders and borrowers: tenants were only 6.5 per cent of enrolled applications. Parametric cover pays fast on a measured trigger but carries basis risk. **Social protection can scale up** by paying more, adding people, relaxing rules or moving entitlements, and each route misses someone.

key_terms.meaning: Splitting losses by frequency and size, with a source for each.
Pradhan Mantri Fasal Bima Yojana, India's crop insurance scheme.
Cover that pays when a measured index crosses a threshold.
Loss without a trigger, or a payout with no loss.
Paying more to people already enrolled in a programme.
Adding affected people who were not enrolled.

worked_example.title: Who does crop insurance reach?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district has 2,000 enrolled PMFBY applications and the share pattern of the deck's 2024-25 figures. Premium for one farmer is ₹1,000, with governments paying 85 per cent.
steps: Tenant farmers at 6.5 per cent: 2,000 × 6.5 ÷ 100 = 130 applications.
Loanee farmers at 48 per cent: 2,000 × 48 ÷ 100 = 960 applications.
Government premium share: 1,000 × 85 ÷ 100 = 850.
The farmer's own premium: 1,000 − 850 = 150.
Landless labourers appear in none of these numbers.
worked_example.answer: 130 tenant and 960 loanee applications out of 2,000, a farmer premium of ₹150, and no cover for landless labourers.

mistakes: Treating crop insurance as protection for everyone hit by drought, when landless labourers are not covered.
Choosing a rainfall index with too few stations, which raises basis risk.
Assuming a State payout helps people without a plan for how it is spent.
Expecting a relaxed rule to apply without the Centre agreeing.

recall.q: Who pays PMFBY premiums, and how much?
recall.a: Union and State governments together pay 85 to 90 per cent.

recall.q: What is basis risk?
recall.a: A household can lose when the index does not trigger, or be paid when it suffered no loss.

recall.q: What was Nagaland's cover?
recall.a: A State-wide parametric policy against extreme rainfall, triggered by automated weather stations.

recall.q: Name the four routes of shock-responsive social protection.
recall.a: Vertical expansion, horizontal expansion, relaxing rules and lending systems or portability.

recall.q: Which instrument fits a long drought's income loss?
recall.a: The rural employment guarantee, which is self-targeting and builds assets.

sections.title: Monitoring preparedness, and sources
sections.big_idea: Judge preparedness from input to impact, **report by group**, and ask what the counterfactual is.
in_plain_words: Preparedness is hard to evaluate because success is a disaster that did less harm than it would have. Choose indicators at four levels: input, output, outcome and impact. The 2025 amendment gives NDMA preparedness assessments and post-disaster audits and requires disaster databases, so more evidence should now exist.

Each method has a limit: before and after comparisons fail when storms differ, and excess mortality needs full death registration. List what your district's data sources already hold before collecting more, because most gaps are in disaggregation by caste, sex, disability and migrant status. **Ask what the counterfactual is**: fewer deaths in a weaker cyclone prove nothing.

worked_example.title: Put numbers on a heat plan framework
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a district of 2,000,000 people had 160 excess deaths in heat alert periods. Of 40 primary health centres, 36 held cooling and oral rehydration stocks on 1 April.
steps: Impact indicator: 160 × 100,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 8 excess deaths per 100,000.
Output 2 indicator: 36 ÷ 40 = 90%.
Both numbers need a source: civil registration for the first, the health checklist for the second.
Add the assumption row: wage protection orders must be in force so workers can stop.
worked_example.answer: 8 excess deaths per 100,000 and 90 per cent of centres ready, each tied to a named source.

mistakes: Reporting fewer deaths after a weaker cyclone as proof that preparedness worked.
Designing new data collection before listing what existing sources hold.
Treating self-reported Sendai figures as a full count of losses.
Leaving the assumptions row out of a results framework.

recall.q: What new evaluation powers does the 2025 amendment give NDMA?
recall.a: Periodic preparedness assessments of each State and post-disaster audits after a severe disaster.

recall.q: What are the four levels of the example indicator table?
recall.a: Input, output, outcome and impact.

recall.q: What is the main limit of NCRB accidental death data?
recall.a: It records only deaths reported to police.

recall.q: Which evaluation method gives the true death toll of an event?
recall.a: Excess mortality, which needs complete death registration.

recall.q: What does the deck say about most data gaps?
recall.a: They are in disaggregation by caste, sex, disability and migrant status.

notes.2: Read the agenda as a staircase from concept to money to hazards to people. Sections 1 to 4 give you the ideas, law and funds, sections 5 to 8 take one hazard family each, and sections 9 to 12 turn to warning, relief, insurance and monitoring.
notes.4: Read the last clause twice: **beyond the coping capacity** of the community. Weather becomes a disaster only when people cannot cope. So when a report blames a cyclone, ask what the people in its path had to protect themselves with.
notes.5: Learn the five terms as a ladder. Hazard is the event, exposure is who stands in its way, vulnerability is how easily they are hurt, risk combines these with capacity, and resilience is the ability to recover. **All five definitions arrived in 2025**, so older papers may use them loosely.
notes.6: Multiply the terms and do not add them. If one falls towards zero, **the product falls towards zero**, which is why moving a village off a floodplain works though the river is unchanged. Note the State shortcut: population stands in for exposure and per-capita income for vulnerability.
notes.7: Use this pair as a template for any case you read. Hold the hazard fixed, then list what differs in exposure and in vulnerability. In village B the warning arrived but nobody came for those who could not walk, so **a warning protects only those it can move**.
notes.8: Read the speed-of-onset column first, because it shapes the response. Days of warning allow evacuation, while seconds of warning for lightning leave only shelter rules and habits. Then match each hazard to your own region and ask which agency produces its district map.
notes.9: Public systems fit events that have a date. The spending shows it: floods took 55.09 per cent of State disaster expenditure and drought 17.26, and **heat was not on the national list at all**. Ask which slow harms in your area have no budget line.
notes.10: Plan for combinations. Pakistan's 2022 floods stacked rain, glacier melt and landslides and affected about 33 million people. Use the table as a prompt: for each hazard you work on, ask what usually follows it and **what it destroys that the next hazard needs**.
notes.11: Keep these five questions on one card and ask them before reading any plan. The last is the sharpest: find the person who cannot read the warning or walk to the shelter and see whether the programme has a **named answer** for them.
notes.13: Take away three facts: adopted 18 March 2015, replaced Hyogo, and voluntary. Of the six shifts in the table, the first matters most: acting on risk before the event. Because nothing binds countries, **reporting against 38 indicators** is where the framework gets its force.
notes.14: Read the goal as three instructions: prevent new risk, reduce existing risk, strengthen resilience. The first is **cheapest and most ignored**, since fast-growing cities create risk now through where they build. The goal names exposure and vulnerability as the things to change, because most hazards cannot be stopped.
notes.15: Sort the seven into two groups. Targets a to d are outcomes, measured with loss data. Targets e to g are means: strategies, cooperation and early warning. Target e has the earlier deadline of 2020, since **strategies had to exist before the outcomes could move**.
notes.16: Memorise the order: understand, govern, invest, prepare. Use it as a checklist on a State plan. If a plan lists response equipment in detail and says nothing under priority 1, it has skipped the step that decides **where the equipment should go**.
notes.17: The framework names five groups you can look for in any plan: disabled people, older persons, migrants, women and indigenous peoples. Caste is missing from the list, yet in South Asia it decides who relief reaches. **Add it to your own checklist.**
notes.18: Sendai progress is self-reported, so quality depends on local records. A country that records few heat deaths looks good on target a whatever is happening. Follow the chain: DesInventar collects, the Monitor reports, and India's 2025 amendment requires databases to **feed that report**.
notes.19: Turn this table into an audit. For each row, ask whether the district keeps the evidence listed. A gap is itself a finding: a district that cannot say how many villages got the last warning has **nothing to show on target g**.
notes.21: Learn the Act as three tiers with a chair at each level: the Prime Minister nationally, the Chief Minister in the State, the Collector in the district. The elected representative is only co-chair at district level. The urban authority, NCMC and **High Level Committee** came in 2025.
notes.22: Read the DDMA's plan and minutes before designing a district programme, since most States publish them. Note the 2025 change that lets civil society members sit on the body. Hold the criticism beside it: a Collector chairs, and the **elected co-chair** had a smaller role in Kerala during COVID-19.
notes.23: A dozen changes in one table, so group them. Vocabulary now matches Sendai. Plans are made by the Authorities themselves. New functions include a disaster database and post-disaster audits. Section 60A gives power over persons. **Read the omissions in ss. 12, 13 and 19** as closely as the additions.
notes.24: Two additions give State and city action a legal base: an urban authority chaired by the Municipal Commissioner, who controls drains and building permits, and a State Disaster Response Force. The Act says States may create both. Watch the initials: **NDRF and SDRF** each mean a force or a fund.
notes.25: Memorise the order: State fund, memorandum, central team, Inter-Ministerial Group, High Level Committee. The State's own money moves at once, while central money waits for four steps. Several States told the Commission that approval and disbursal were delayed, so ask **how long people in camps waited**.
notes.26: Two promises sit here: minimum standards of relief and no discrimination on sex, caste, community, descent or religion. The 2025 text dropped "compensation" from s. 61 and does not list disability, age or migrant status. **Cite s. 61 as it now stands** when documenting exclusion.
notes.27: Treat plans as the working layer of the law. Use the slide's test: does the plan name people and places, or only departments and phone numbers? District plans must now be reviewed at least every two years. **Heat action plans are not created by the Act**, and section 8 returns to this.
notes.28: Hold both readings together. The government stresses clarity and data. Chathukulam sees centralisation. A database or audit power is useful, and **who controls it decides whom it serves**. Then put the slide's three questions to your own State: urban authority, published database, panchayat plans and money.
notes.30: Four funds, two levels, two jobs: response funds pay for relief and mitigation funds pay for prevention projects. Remember the shares: Union 75 and State 25, or 90:10 for north-eastern and Himalayan States. **District funds exist on paper only**, as the Fifteenth Commission found them impractical.
notes.31: You need not memorise ten rows. Remember the arc: margin money (Second), a fund with a Union share (Ninth), merger into SDRF and NDRF under the Act (Thirteenth), a 10 per cent local window (Fourteenth), mitigation funds (**Fifteenth**). Each Commission tried to correct the last.
notes.32: Each award is larger than the last, reaching ₹2,04,401 crore for State funds in 2026-31. Remember the slide's caveat: the figures are nominal allocations. Before you quote growth as progress, **ask what was released and what was spent**.
notes.33: Two parts: 70 per cent on past spending and 30 per cent on a risk index. Read the consequence column. A State that under-spent on heat or drought is not compensated, and per-capita income hides poor districts. Check Annexures 11.3 and 11.4 before **claiming winners and losers**.
notes.34: Compare old and new. Both keep 80:20 between response and mitigation. FC-16 gives States free movement between relief and recovery and shifts preparedness into the mitigation funds. Money **cannot cross** between response and mitigation, because they are separate funds under the Act.
notes.35: Mitigation money exists and is slow: central releases ran near 80 per cent of allocation against 95 to 100 for response funds. The slide calls this an opening. A district proposal with a **hazard, a costed project and a monitoring plan** is what these funds were waiting for.
notes.36: More than half of relief spending went on agricultural inputs and 23.4 per cent on ex gratia. Both lines reach landholders and the families of the dead. **Landless wage workers and sick people** sit in neither, so read any relief budget for who is missing.
notes.37: Know the notified list and its gap. Heat and lightning are off it, though 11 States treat heat as a State disaster and 16 treat lightning so. The 10 per cent window pays for them. Check the current MHA list, since **a recommendation is a separate step** from a notification.
notes.39: Odisha is a test case because high hazard meets high vulnerability: poor, rural, with Scheduled Tribes and Castes together 39.9 per cent in 2011. When deaths fall under those conditions, the system is worth studying. Note the geography: 260 of 890 east coast landfalls reached **this one coast**.
notes.40: Read the table as one system and not a shopping list: a standing authority, a rescue force, shelters linked to community task forces, sirens to the last mile and an operations centre that runs all year. Odisha built these after 1999, **before the national Act existed**, over two decades.
notes.41: Deaths fell from nearly 10,000 to 44, none, 61 and 64. The slide supplies two cautions: storms differ, and the record cannot say which component saved lives. Keep the other half too. **Zero mortality is close but losses are rising**, about USD 5.7 billion for three storms.
notes.42: Walk the timeline and notice that each step is a decision by a named office. Eleven days of warning let officials stock grain and move pregnant women. Test your own plan with the slide's rule: does **every decision have a trigger, an owner and a deadline**?
notes.43: These numbers describe reach: 15.5 lakh people moved, 1.8 crore SMS alerts, sirens and radio in Odia. Notice the layers, and that Collectors were told to move older and disabled people, women and children. Compare it with your district's list of **who needs help moving**.
notes.44: Eight of the affected districts reported no deaths, 64 in total, yet damage reached ₹16,465 crore and recovery needs ₹29,315 crore. Low deaths and high losses fall on the same people, in kutcha houses. Remember the report calls its figures **conservative**.
notes.45: The state's own report found two failures. Cash and rice tied to ration cards excluded migrants and brick kiln workers, and shelters were segregated by a dominant class. **A system that saves lives can share relief unequally.** The fixes: relief without proof of residency, and shelters nearer Dalit hamlets.
notes.46: Read the last two rows as unfinished work. The first five, about saving lives, travel to other coasts. Livelihoods and dignity need local adaptation: shelters sited near the poorest hamlets and **relief that reaches people missing from the ration card system**.
notes.48: Floods take most of the money, but a flood is not one thing. Match the response to the clock: days for rivers and surge, minutes for flash floods, hours for urban floods. Costs fall mainly on crops, houses and roads, and **deaths are the smaller part**.
notes.49: Treat an embankment as protection for some and a hazard for others. People living between it and the river get the worst floods, and a breach floods land believed safe. Use the four questions, especially the last: **a breach needs its own warning plan**.
notes.50: Remember the poverty number: floods that killed more than 1,700 people could push 8.4 to 9.1 million into poverty, with about 33 million affected. **Counting deaths alone misses most of the harm**, so check what any assessment you read measured beyond deaths.
notes.51: Landslides take 2.59 per cent of spending because hill States are small, which says little about their danger. Look at the table: the landslide and seismic lines had almost nothing released by July 2025. **Rainfall thresholds** are the working warning tool.
notes.52: Lightning led natural deaths in 2022, with 2,887 of 8,060. Vulnerability here is about work, since labourers in open fields have no shelter. An SMS reaches phone owners, while a field worker needs **a siren, a nearby shelter and an employer who lets them stop**.
notes.53: Relief follows what is counted. Crop loss is measured carefully, so inputs took 55.6 per cent of relief, while lost wages are rarely measured. Use the table to see what each source misses and add **days of work lost** whenever you design an assessment.
notes.54: Use these five asks as a field kit: ten years of flooded villages, embankment repair dates, landslide thresholds, lightning warnings that reach field workers, and mitigation fund proposals. They turn general worry into **records to request and people to visit**. The Climate Risk and Adaptation Studio lets you practise.
notes.56: Drought arrives in stages: rain fails, crops fail weeks later, wells fail months later, and people sell animals and borrow throughout. Pick the declaration trigger with care. Rainfall alone is early and can miss badly timed rain, while waiting for crop-cutting is late. **Work and food over months** matter most.
notes.57: Drought is second in State spending at 17.26 per cent, and most agricultural input subsidy is paid here. Subsidy reaches cultivators, while the labourers who lose the most work **need a different instrument**. Note the earmark: ₹350 crore of ₹1,200 crore released.
notes.58: This slide records a law change: the old rural employment Act was repealed from 1 July 2026 and the new Act guarantees at least 125 days. States must also notify sixty peak-season days with no work. Sections 7(1) and 7(2) allow **relaxations in a calamity**, so read them before a drought.
notes.59: A declaration decides who gets help, so ask five design questions: how small the unit, how early, whether relief needs land records, whether jobs expand at once, and whether migrants are counted. The slide says the **current procedure was not verified**, so read the latest text.
notes.60: Use this list as a monitoring dashboard. Each indicator moves before crop-cutting results arrive: work demanded, fodder prices, livestock sales, migration, school attendance, debt, tanker queues. Together they show whether a response **reaches people**, which input subsidy payments alone cannot.
notes.62: Memorise the plains numbers: 40°C basic, 45°C for a heat wave and 47°C for severe. Declaration needs two stations for two days. The slide's lesson is that dry temperature is blunt for health, which is why **local thresholds** matter; only ten of 37 plans set them.
notes.63: Hot days and warm nights both matter, since warm nights stop the body recovering and raise heatstroke risk. Use the table as a starting list, then do what CPR says most plans skip: a **local vulnerability assessment** that finds where those people actually live.
notes.64: Humidity changes the danger. Wet-bulb temperature combines heat and humidity, and sweating stops working as it nears skin temperature. Chamber tests on young healthy adults found limits near 30.55°C in humid heat, **below the 35°C theory**, so older people and heavy workers reach their limits sooner.
notes.65: Learn the method as much as the number: 1,344 excess deaths, 43.1 per cent, found by comparing all deaths in May 2010 with 2009 and 2011. **None were recorded as heat deaths.** Counting heatstroke certificates would have found a small fraction.
notes.66: Read the plan as a chain from forecast to review. A 7-day probabilistic forecast triggers alerts, hospitals and water points prepare, messages reach workers and slums, and the season ends with a **review of deaths**. Note the 2017 addition of cool roofs for slum residents.
notes.67: Read the uncertainty as carefully as the headline. The estimate is 1,190 avoided deaths a year, but the interval runs from 162 to 2,218. It is one city compared before and after, so other changes could explain part of the fall. **Call it pilot evidence**, as the authors do.
notes.68: Four findings sum up 37 plans: thresholds are rarely local, vulnerable groups are poorly targeted, funding is thin and none names its legal authority. Take the fix from the recommendations: **link each action to a law or scheme** so that someone is obliged and funded to carry it out.
notes.69: The two numbers answer different questions. NCRB counted 3,798 heat deaths nationally in five years, while one Ahmedabad month showed 1,344 excess deaths. Undercounting makes heat look small, gets it **less money** and makes the Sendai mortality target look met.
notes.70: Heat is an income shock before it is a health emergency. The ILO projects India's lost working hours rising from 4.3 per cent in 1995 to 5.8 in 2030, about 34 million full-time jobs. The estimate assumes shade, so **real losses for field and site workers are larger**.
notes.71: Agriculture and construction carry most of the loss, and brick kilns are the extreme case, with workers exposed to 40 to 45°C air and radiant heat. The ILO found the relevant statutes unclear for kiln workers. **Labour law has changed since**, so check what applies in your State.
notes.72: Treat this as a seven-step checklist, each row answering a weakness the review found. The evidence column is the useful part: ask for the threshold table, the ward list, the signed procedures and the **monthly excess-death analysis** before accepting that a plan exists.
notes.74: Think of five links: forecast, warning, dissemination, understanding and action. Find the weakest link with the typical-failure column. The key words in Sendai target g are **access to**: an accurate forecast that reaches only smartphone owners in English is no early warning for rural South Asia.
notes.75: Warnings travel along the lines of ordinary inequality, so match each group to a channel that reaches it. The Collector's order to move vulnerable people works only if **a list of those people, by village**, already exists. The simplest form is a list of who needs a visit.
notes.76: Define anticipatory action by its three parts: pre-agreed steps, money set aside in advance and a forecast threshold. The Fani list shows it at work. The cost is spending on a hazard that proves **weaker than forecast**, a price worth naming before the season starts.
notes.77: Fill in one row per hazard before the season: the forecast, the lead time, the action and the cost if the forecast is wrong. Remember the last sentence: **a system with no false alarms is probably acting too late**. Write the cost of acting in vain in advance.
notes.78: Warning systems trade two errors. Low thresholds give false alarms and lost wages, and after a few of those people stop leaving. High thresholds miss events. Fani's track changed nine times, yet evacuation began at confirmed landfall with time left. **Compensate people for the cost of acting.**
notes.79: Use this table as an evaluation plan for any warning system, each question with an indicator and a source. The hard and useful part is disaggregation: a **90 per cent average can hide a hamlet that received nothing**. Add the death audit to learn who was left out.
notes.81: Keep the four terms apart: response saves lives, rehabilitation restores services, recovery restores or improves assets, reconstruction rebuilds. Note the money gap, with the recovery window at ₹818.74 crore released of ₹20,539 crore. The word **improvement** in recovery is the legal hook for Build Back Better.
notes.82: This is evidence that relief can follow social hierarchy. HRW reported fishing communities blocking aid from Dalits, and farm labourers who lost crops and wages were ignored because fewer died. Fifteen years later, Fani shelters showed segregation again. HRW's conclusion: **proactive government measures** are needed.
notes.83: Read the table as practice, effect, alternative. The root cause was ration cards in the male head's name, so women's aid passed through men. Fixes include individual registration, counting women's fishery work, private toilets, **joint title** and women on every committee.
notes.84: Relief runs on lists, and anyone off the list is invisible. After Fani, cash and rice went to ration card holders only, excluding migrants and kiln workers. The new rural employment law offers a model, with **job cards at the place of relocation**. The first step is to count migrants before the disaster.
notes.85: Disasters hurt people with disabilities disproportionately and create new disabilities. Use the five steps as a village checklist, starting with a list of people who need help to evacuate and **a named person for each**. Section 61 names sex, caste, community, descent and religion, and omits disability and age.
notes.86: Use this as an audit of any relief operation. Each of the seven principles comes from a failure recorded in India: discrimination, women paid through men, residence tests, flat quantities, uncounted indirect losses, inaccessible shelters and no voice in recovery. **Score a scheme against all seven** before praising it.
notes.88: Match the money to the layer. Small frequent losses come from savings and budgets, medium ones from State funds, and rare large ones from insurance and bonds. India leans on public funds, and insurance is nascent apart from crop cover. Governments prefer to **pay after a disaster** than buy cover before.
notes.89: PMFBY is large, with governments paying 85 to 90 per cent of premium, yet penetration reached only 40 per cent in eight years. Tenants made up 6.5 per cent of enrolled applications and loanee farmers 48. **Crop insurance protects people with land and loans**, and landless labourers are not covered.
notes.90: Parametric insurance pays when an index crosses a threshold, so it pays fast. Its weakness is **basis risk**: a household can lose and not be paid, or be paid with no loss. Use the five design questions. Nagaland's State-wide rainfall cover is the example, called a success that remains isolated.
notes.91: Four routes let existing programmes scale in a shock: pay more to those enrolled, add new people, relax rules, or let entitlements move with the person. Each misses someone, as the third column shows. **Horizontal expansion needs a way to identify people fast.**
notes.92: Use the table to match need to instrument, then combine. Cash comes from a top-up, long-drought income from the employment guarantee, crop loss from PMFBY, State liquidity from parametric cover. The slide's closing example: a family needs **a top-up in week one, work in month two, a house in year one**.
notes.94: Preparedness is hard to evaluate because success looks like harm that did not happen. Use the four-level table to choose indicators from input to impact. The 2025 amendment gives NDMA preparedness assessments and **post-disaster audits**, and requires databases, so the evidence you need may now be created by law.
notes.95: Choose a method for each question and note its limit. Before and after comparisons fail when storms differ, and excess mortality needs full death registration. Report results by group, since systems that cut total deaths can still exclude Dalits, migrants, women and disabled people. **Always ask for the counterfactual.**
notes.96: Before designing new data collection, list what these sources already hold for your district. Each has a catch: NDMIS depends on State entry, NCRB records only police-reported deaths, DesInventar is self-reported. Most gaps lie in **disaggregation** by caste, sex, disability and migrant status.
notes.97: This is a template to copy. Read it from the bottom: outputs deliver outcomes, which deliver the impact. The assumption row is the one people skip: **workers cannot stop in a heatwave without wage protection**. Every indicator names a source, so the whole framework can be audited.
notes.98: This is the reference list for the first half of the course: the Sendai text, the DM Acts, the Finance Commission report, the Odisha and Pakistan assessments. Go to the original when you quote a figure, since the **Finance Commission report** is the source for most of the funding numbers.
notes.99: The second half lists the heat and labour sources: IMD definitions, the Ahmedabad papers, the wet-bulb studies, the ILO report, the CPR review, HRW's tsunami report and the rural employment Act. Check each date before quoting, since the deck notes that **labour law has changed** since the ILO report.
